title: Certified Kubernetes Administrator
description: Unofficial knowledge practice mapped to the published CKA curriculum (Kubernetes v1.35). The real exam is a 2-hour performance-based lab with kubernetes.io docs; these items are not Linux Foundation exam questions.

questions.objective: Manage role based access control (RBAC)
questions.stem: A ServiceAccount `deployer` in namespace `cicd` must create Deployments only in `cicd`. Which pair is the smallest RBAC that does that?
questions.explanation: A namespaced Role plus RoleBinding grants verbs in one namespace. ClusterRoleBinding would apply cluster-wide. A ClusterRole can be RoleBound into one namespace, but a RoleBinding to a ClusterRole is extra scope you do not need if the rules are namespace-local. Binding a ClusterRole cluster-wide (c) is too broad. A RoleBinding cannot reference a Role in another namespace (d).

choices.text: Role in `cicd` plus RoleBinding of `deployer` to that Role
RoleBinding in `default` pointing at a Role in `cicd`
ClusterRoleBinding to a ClusterRole named edit

questions.objective: Manage role based access control (RBAC)
questions.stem: A Pod must call the API as itself. Which field on the Pod spec selects the identity?
questions.explanation: `spec.serviceAccountName` selects the ServiceAccount whose token kubelet mounts. fsGroup is filesystem group, not API identity. imagePullSecrets are registry creds. automountServiceAccountToken: false disables the token, it does not choose which SA.

questions.objective: Manage role based access control (RBAC)
questions.stem: A user must `get` and `list` Nodes. Which object holds those rules?
questions.explanation: Node is cluster-scoped, so the rules live in a ClusterRole (then ClusterRoleBinding). A Role can only name namespaced resources. RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding attach subjects to roles; they do not hold the verb lists. An empty RoleBinding grants nothing.

questions.objective: Create and manage Kubernetes clusters using kubeadm
questions.stem: After `kubeadm init`, a control-plane node’s API server is a static Pod. Where does kubelet look for that manifest by default?
questions.explanation: kubeadm writes static Pod manifests under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`. kubelet’s `--pod-manifest-path` (or `staticPodPath`) defaults there. `/var/lib/kubelet` is runtime state. `/etc/kubernetes/pki` is certificates. `/opt/cni/bin` is CNI plugins.

questions.objective: Create and manage Kubernetes clusters using kubeadm
questions.stem: A worker should join a kubeadm cluster. The bootstrap token expired. Which kubeadm command mints a new join token on a control-plane node?
questions.explanation: `kubeadm token create --print-join-command` prints a fresh `kubeadm join …`. `kubeadm init` would try to bootstrap a new cluster. `kubeadm reset` tears a node down. `kubeadm upgrade apply` upgrades the current node, it does not print a join command.

questions.objective: Manage the lifecycle of Kubernetes clusters
questions.stem: You are upgrading a kubeadm cluster one minor version. Which order matches the documented control-plane then workers flow?
questions.explanation: Documented flow: upgrade control planes (`upgrade apply` then `upgrade node`), then workers (`upgrade node`), including kubelet. Workers first breaks API compatibility. kubeadm init is bootstrap, not upgrade. Skipping kubelet while only rolling kube-proxy leaves the node on an old kubelet.

choices.text: All workers first, then the control plane
kube-proxy DaemonSet only, then skip kubelet packages
Run `kubeadm init` again on every node
Control plane nodes, then worker nodes

questions.objective: Manage the lifecycle of Kubernetes clusters
questions.stem: Stacked etcd on the first control-plane node must be snapshotted before an upgrade. Which tool and subcommand writes the snapshot file?
questions.explanation: `etcdctl snapshot save <file>` is the documented backup. `kubeadm init` does not snapshot. `kubectl get etcd` is not a backup. `crictl checkpoint` checkpoints containers, not the etcd datastore.

references.title: Kubernetes docs — etcd backup and restore

questions.objective: Manage the lifecycle of Kubernetes clusters
questions.stem: You restored an etcd snapshot onto a stacked control plane. What else must typically be true for the API server to use that data?
questions.explanation: After `etcdctl snapshot restore`, etcd must be restarted with the restored data dir (and matching `--initial-cluster` flags as documented). Restoring only a kubeconfig or only the scheduler manifest does not replace etcd data. CNI restart is unrelated.

references.title: Kubernetes docs — etcd backup and restore

choices.text: Point etcd at the restored data directory and restart etcd/static Pod

questions.objective: Implement and configure a highly-available control plane
questions.stem: A kubeadm HA cluster has three stacked control-plane nodes. How should kubelets and `kubectl` reach the API so one CP failure is survivable?
questions.explanation: HA topology docs put a load balancer (or DNS with health checks) in front of the control-plane endpoints; kubeadm `--control-plane-endpoint` is that stable address. Pointing every kubelet at a single node IP (b) is a single point of failure. NodePort 30000 is for Services, not the API. etcd peer URLs are not the Kubernetes API.

choices.text: A load-balanced `--control-plane-endpoint` in front of the three API servers
A NodePort Service on 30000 targeting kube-apiserver
Every kubelet `--kubeconfig` using the first node’s IP only
Clients talking to etcd peer ports instead of the API

questions.objective: Implement and configure a highly-available control plane
questions.stem: In kubeadm stacked etcd HA, each control-plane node runs kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, and a local etcd member.
questions.explanation: Stacked etcd colocates an etcd member with each control-plane instance. External etcd is the other documented topology, with etcd on separate hosts. True is the stacked definition.

questions.objective: Use Helm and Kustomize to install cluster components
questions.stem: A Helm release `ingress` is already installed. You need to apply a new chart version and keep the same release name. Which command is the documented path?
questions.explanation: `helm upgrade` (often `upgrade --install`) updates an existing release. `helm install` fails if the name exists. `helm rollback` goes to a previous revision, not a newer chart. `helm repo add` only registers a repo.

questions.objective: Use Helm and Kustomize to install cluster components
questions.stem: A directory contains `kustomization.yaml` plus base manifests. Which kubectl invocation applies that overlay?
questions.explanation: `kubectl apply -k <dir>` builds the overlay. `-f kustomization.yaml` applies that file as a raw object, it does not build bases. `replace --force -f .` is a delete/recreate of files as-is. `patch -k` is not how you apply an overlay.

questions.objective: Understand extension interfaces (CNI, CSI, CRI, etc.)
questions.stem: A cluster was just created with kubeadm. Nodes never become Ready and CoreDNS Pods stay Pending. kubelet and containerd are running. What is still missing?
questions.explanation: kubeadm does not install a Pod network. Until a CNI plugin is applied, Nodes stay NotReady for networking and CoreDNS cannot run. CSI is storage. CRI (containerd) is already running in this scenario. A default StorageClass is unrelated.

choices.text: A CSI driver is not installed
A CNI plugin (Pod network) is not installed

questions.objective: Understand extension interfaces (CNI, CSI, CRI, etc.)
questions.stem: kubelet talks to the container runtime through which interface?
questions.explanation: kubelet talks to the runtime through CRI (containerd, CRI-O). CNI is networking. CSI is volumes. An OCI runtime is what the CRI implementation calls; kubelet does not speak OCI instead of CRI.

choices.text: the OCI runtime spec only, with no kubelet CRI client

questions.objective: Understand extension interfaces (CNI, CSI, CRI, etc.)
questions.stem: Dynamic provisioning from a StorageClass named `fast` failed with “no volume plugin matched”. The class’s `provisioner` field names a driver. Which extension interface must be running for that provisioner?
questions.explanation: StorageClass.provisioner is a CSI (or in-tree) volume plugin. CNI will not provision disks. CRI runs containers. RBAC may block the provisioner SA, but the error “no volume plugin matched” is a missing CSI/in-tree plugin, not a Role.

questions.objective: Understand CRDs, install and configure operators
questions.stem: An Operator installs a new `Backup` API. After install, `kubectl get backups` works. Which object registered that API with the apiserver?
questions.explanation: A CustomResourceDefinition registers a new kind with the API. A ConfigMap cannot add APIs. MutatingWebhookConfiguration intercepts existing APIs. A Service exposes endpoints, it does not register kinds.

choices.text: Service of type ClusterIP named backups

questions.objective: Understand CRDs, install and configure operators
questions.stem: You installed an Operator that watches `Backup` CRs. The Operator process itself should run as which workload so it survives node loss and is upgraded via a rolling update?
questions.explanation: Operators are typically Deployments so replicas reschedule and roll. A naked Pod is not self-healing. A Job runs to completion. A StatefulSet can run a controller but is the wrong default for a stateless operator process.

choices.text: A StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates for etcd-like identity
A single Pod with no controller

questions.objective: Manage the lifecycle of Kubernetes clusters
questions.stem: kubeadm-issued control-plane certificates are nearing expiry. Which command renews them on a control-plane node?
questions.explanation: `kubeadm certs renew all` (or a named cert) is the documented renewal. `kubeadm init` is bootstrap. `kubectl delete secret` in default does not rotate apiserver certs. `kubeadm join` adds a node.

questions.objective: Prepare underlying infrastructure for installing a Kubernetes cluster
questions.stem: On a control-plane node, which TCP port must be reachable for the Kubernetes API server (default)?
questions.explanation: kube-apiserver’s default secure port is 6443. 10250 is kubelet, 2379 is etcd client, 10259 is scheduler.

questions.objective: Prepare underlying infrastructure for installing a Kubernetes cluster
questions.stem: Which TCP port is the default etcd client port that kube-apiserver uses?
questions.explanation: etcd client API is 2379; peer is 2380. 6443 is kube-apiserver. 10250 is kubelet.

references.title: Kubernetes docs — etcd backup and restore

questions.objective: Prepare underlying infrastructure for installing a Kubernetes cluster
questions.stem: Which TCP port does kubelet listen on by default for the kubelet API?
questions.explanation: kubelet’s default HTTPS port is 10250. 6443 is the API server. 10256 is kube-proxy health. 2379 is etcd.

questions.objective: Create and manage Kubernetes clusters using kubeadm
questions.stem: A node must leave a kubeadm cluster and be reinstalled. Which command on that node stops kubelet and cleans kubeadm state?
questions.explanation: `kubeadm reset` is the documented teardown. `kubectl delete node` only removes the API object; you still reset the node. `systemctl stop docker` is the wrong runtime and incomplete. `kubeadm init` bootstraps.

choices.text: `kubectl delete node` only, on the node itself

questions.objective: Understand application deployments and how to perform rolling update and rollbacks
questions.stem: A Deployment `web` just rolled out a bad image. You want the previous ReplicaSet back. Which command is the documented rollback?
questions.explanation: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` restores the prior revision. Deleting the Deployment removes the app. `scale --replicas=0` is not a rollback. `rollout pause` freezes, it does not revert.

questions.objective: Understand application deployments and how to perform rolling update and rollbacks
questions.stem: You applied a new image and need to wait until the rollout is healthy before the next change. Which command blocks until the Deployment is complete?
questions.explanation: `kubectl rollout status` waits for the rollout to finish (or errors). `get pods -w` never decides “complete”. `describe` is a snapshot. `logs -f` tails one container.

questions.objective: Understand application deployments and how to perform rolling update and rollbacks
questions.stem: A Deployment uses `RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 1`. During an update, what is guaranteed?
questions.explanation: maxUnavailable=0 means desired pods stay up; maxSurge=1 allows one extra Pod. Together that is a surge-then-replace rollout with no capacity drop. maxUnavailable=0 does not mean zero downtime if probes fail (c). It does not recreate every node (d). It is the opposite of killing all old pods first (b).

choices.text: At least the desired replica count stays up; one extra Pod may exist
The Service cannot fail any request even if readiness probes fail
All old Pods are deleted before any new Pod starts

questions.objective: Use ConfigMaps and Secrets to configure applications
questions.stem: A ConfigMap `app-config` has key `LOG_LEVEL`. The container should see that as an environment variable of the same name. Which Pod spec form is the usual mapping?
questions.explanation: `env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` (or `envFrom.configMapRef`) injects ConfigMap keys as env. Mounting as a volume puts files in a directory, not env. `kubectl set env` from a Secret is the wrong object. Downward API exposes pod fields, not ConfigMap keys.

choices.text: volumeMount of the ConfigMap at `/etc/env` only

questions.objective: Use ConfigMaps and Secrets to configure applications
questions.stem: A TLS key in Secret `web-tls` must appear as a file in the container, not as an environment variable. How should the Pod consume it?
questions.explanation: Secrets (and ConfigMaps) can be projected as volumes; that is the right way for files/keys. envFrom puts values in the environment (and is discouraged for credentials in process listings). imagePullSecrets only pull images. hostPath would read a node file, not the Secret object.

choices.text: A volume of `secret.secretName: web-tls` and a volumeMount

questions.objective: Configure workload autoscaling
questions.stem: An HPA targets Deployment `api` at 70% CPU. The HPA stays at the minimum replicas and never scales up even under load. CPU usage in `kubectl top pod` looks high. What is the usual missing piece on the Pod template?
questions.explanation: HPA CPU utilization is current/requests. Without requests, that ratio is undefined. limits cap runtime, they are not the HPA denominator. A PDB is disruption. LimitRange is admission, not the HPA metric.

choices.text: CPU limits only, with no CPU requests

questions.objective: Understand the primitives used to create robust, self-healing, application deployments
questions.stem: A Pod is Running and the container has started, but it stays off the Service. `kubectl get endpoints` is empty for that Pod. Which probe is failing?
questions.explanation: Readiness gates Service membership. Liveness kills/restarts the container (you would see restarts). Startup delays the other probes during boot. A node Ready condition is not a container probe.

questions.objective: Understand the primitives used to create robust, self-healing, application deployments
questions.stem: A container is stuck: it accepts TCP but deadlocks. You want kubelet to restart that container. Which probe should you add?
questions.explanation: livenessProbe failure restarts the container. readinessProbe only removes it from endpoints. preStop runs on shutdown, it does not detect a deadlock. startupProbe only covers boot; after it succeeds you still need liveness for a later hang.

choices.text: startupProbe only, with no livenessProbe after start

questions.objective: Understand the primitives used to create robust, self-healing, application deployments
questions.stem: You need exactly one Pod on every node, including future nodes. Which controller?
questions.explanation: DaemonSet schedules one Pod per eligible node. Deployment uses a replica count, not per-node. StatefulSet is ordered identity. ReplicaSet is the Deployment backend, still replica-count based.

choices.text: Deployment with replicas equal to the current node count

questions.objective: Understand the primitives used to create robust, self-healing, application deployments
questions.stem: An app needs stable network identity (`web-0`, `web-1`) and a dedicated PVC per replica. Which controller?
questions.explanation: StatefulSet gives stable names, a headless Service, and volumeClaimTemplates. Deployment Pods are interchangeable. DaemonSet is per-node. CronJob is time-based Jobs.

questions.objective: Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, etc.)
questions.stem: Control-plane nodes have taint `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`. A logging DaemonSet must run there too. What does the DaemonSet Pod spec need?
questions.explanation: A matching toleration lets the Pod schedule onto the tainted node. nodeSelector alone does not override NoSchedule. Privileged is a securityContext, not a taint bypass. HostNetwork is not a toleration.

questions.objective: Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, etc.)
questions.stem: Pods of Deployment `cache` must land only on nodes labeled `disk=ssd`. Which scheduling field enforces that hard constraint?
questions.explanation: requiredDuringScheduling nodeAffinity (or a matching nodeSelector) is a hard rule. preferredDuringScheduling is a hint. podAntiAffinity is about other pods. Topology spread is evenness, not a label allow-list.

questions.objective: Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, etc.)
questions.stem: A Pod stays Pending with “Insufficient cpu”. The node has free CPU but less than the Pod asked. Which Pod spec field is the scheduler comparing?
questions.explanation: The scheduler matches `resources.requests` against leftover node allocatable. limits are not the scheduling number (they cap runtime). Huge pages are a different resource. priorityClassName affects preemption order, not the CPU arithmetic itself.

questions.objective: Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, etc.)
questions.stem: Every container in namespace `team` must get a default CPU request if the Pod omits one. Which namespaced object sets that default?
questions.explanation: LimitRange `defaultRequest` (and default limits) applies at admission in a namespace. ResourceQuota caps totals, it does not inject requests. LimitRange is not a ClusterRole. HPA scales replicas, it does not default CPU requests.

questions.objective: Understand application deployments and how to perform rolling update and rollbacks
questions.stem: You must change only the image of Deployment `web` to `org/web:1.4` without hand-editing YAML. Which kubectl command is the usual one-liner?
questions.explanation: `kubectl set image` patches the named container image. replace --force deletes/recreates. scale changes replica count, not the image. annotate does not change the image field.

questions.objective: Understand application deployments and how to perform rolling update and rollbacks
questions.stem: You need to see prior ReplicaSet revisions of Deployment `web` before picking a rollback target. Which command lists them?
questions.explanation: `kubectl rollout history deployment/web` prints revisions. `get rs` shows ReplicaSets but not the Deployment revision table. `logs --previous` is a crashed container. `auth can-i` is RBAC.

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: If a Service spec omits `spec.type`, Kubernetes treats it as ClusterIP.
questions.explanation: ClusterIP is the default Service type. NodePort and LoadBalancer must be set explicitly. True is the documented default.

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: Pods in the cluster must reach `web` on port 80 using a stable IP that is not on a node. Which Service type?
questions.explanation: ClusterIP is an in-cluster virtual IP. NodePort also allocates a host port. LoadBalancer asks for an external LB. ExternalName is a DNS CNAME, not a cluster IP.

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: You create a Service `type: NodePort` without setting `nodePort`. Which range does kube-apiserver pick from by default?
questions.explanation: The default NodePort range is 30000–32767 (`service-node-port-range`). 80–443 are host HTTP. 10250 is kubelet. 6443 is the API server.

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: On a cloud cluster, clients on the internet must hit the Service without picking a node IP. Which type asks the cloud for an address?
questions.explanation: LoadBalancer provisions an external address via the cloud integration. ClusterIP is internal. NodePort needs a node IP plus the high port. Headless (`clusterIP: None`) returns Pod IPs, not an LB.

choices.text: NodePort only, with no cloud integration

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: A Service selector matches no Pods. What do you expect on its Endpoints/EndpointSlice?
questions.explanation: No matching Ready Pods means empty EndpointSlices; the Service object (and ClusterIP, if any) still exists. kube-proxy does not invent backends. CoreDNS still resolves the Service name to the ClusterIP. Creation of the Service does not require backends.

choices.text: The Service has no ClusterIP until a Pod exists
CoreDNS refuses to resolve the Service name
The Service object cannot be created

questions.objective: Define and enforce Network Policies
questions.stem: Namespace `prod` has a NetworkPolicy that selects all Pods and allows ingress only from Pods labeled `role=frontend`. A Pod labeled `role=db` in `prod` sends TCP to another Pod. What happens to that connection?
questions.explanation: Once a NetworkPolicy selects a Pod, unmatched ingress is denied. Same-namespace is not an implicit allow. A dest Pod does not need its own policy object. Omitting policyTypes still defaults to Ingress, so that is not an allow.

choices.text: It is allowed because both Pods share a namespace
It is dropped; the dest Pod is isolated except from `role=frontend`
The packet is allowed because policyTypes omitted Ingress
It is allowed because the dest Pod has no policy object of its own

questions.objective: Define and enforce Network Policies
questions.stem: You must stop Pods labeled `app=batch` from initiating connections except to a CIDR of `10.0.0.0/8`. Which NetworkPolicy stanza enforces that?
questions.explanation: egress + podSelector restricts outbound. ingress only affects incoming. ExternalName does not implement NetworkPolicy. An ingress-only policy leaves egress unrestricted (default allow for unselected directions).

choices.text: An ingress-only policy with no egress rules
Change the Service type to ExternalName

questions.objective: Know how to use Ingress controllers and Ingress resources
questions.stem: HTTP hosts `a.example.com` and `b.example.com` should route to different Services on one external HTTP port. Which API object is the classic per-cluster L7 route (before Gateway API)?
questions.explanation: Ingress maps host/path to Services via an Ingress controller. A NodePort is L4 per service. NetworkPolicy is not HTTP routing. EndpointSlice is backend addresses.

questions.objective: Know how to use Ingress controllers and Ingress resources
questions.stem: Creating an Ingress object is enough to serve traffic; Kubernetes always includes a working Ingress controller in every cluster.
questions.explanation: Ingress is data. An Ingress controller (ingress-nginx, cloud LB, etc.) must be installed. kubeadm clusters do not ship one by default. False is correct.

questions.objective: Use the Gateway API to manage Ingress traffic
questions.stem: Using Gateway API, which object typically describes HTTP path routing to a backend Service?
questions.explanation: HTTPRoute (Gateway API) attaches to a Gateway and routes HTTP. Gateway is the listener/infra. Ingress is the older API. NetworkPolicy is not HTTP routing.

questions.objective: Use the Gateway API to manage Ingress traffic
questions.stem: A cluster already has Ingress objects. You are asked to adopt Gateway API for new HTTP routes. Which statement matches the docs?
questions.explanation: Gateway API (Gateway + HTTPRoute) can coexist with Ingress. You do not have to delete Ingress objects. HTTPRoute is its own kind. Gateway API includes HTTP routing, not only TCP.

choices.text: Gateway API is only for non-HTTP TCP and cannot route HTTP
Gateway API objects replace IngressClass but you must delete every Ingress first
HTTPRoute is a field on Ingress, not a separate kind
New routes can use Gateway/HTTPRoute; existing Ingress can keep working

questions.objective: Understand and use CoreDNS
questions.stem: Pods cannot resolve `kubernetes.default.svc`. Which namespace is CoreDNS installed in on a typical kubeadm cluster?
questions.explanation: CoreDNS runs in `kube-system` (Deployment/Service `kube-dns`). `kube-public` is for public cluster info. `kube-node-lease` is leases. `default` is the user default namespace.

questions.objective: Understand and use CoreDNS
questions.stem: From a Pod in namespace `shop`, which name reaches Service `api` in the same namespace via cluster DNS?
questions.explanation: Short name `api` works in the same namespace (search path). FQDN is `api.shop.svc.cluster.local`. `api.kube-system` is the wrong namespace. `api.default.svc` is default, not shop.

questions.objective: Understand connectivity between Pods
questions.stem: Two Pods on different nodes communicate using Pod IPs. Which component provides that overlay or routing?
questions.explanation: The CNI plugin implements Pod-to-Pod networking. kube-proxy is Services/NAT, not Pod IP routing. CoreDNS is names. The scheduler does not forward packets.

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: A ClusterIP Service is created. Which node component programs iptables or IPVS so traffic to that VIP reaches Pods?
questions.explanation: kube-proxy watches Services/EndpointSlices and programs iptables or IPVS (or nft). kubelet runs Pods. CoreDNS answers DNS. etcd stores data, it does not NAT.

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: A StatefulSet needs DNS A/AAAA records for each Pod (`web-0.web`). Which Service setting is required?
questions.explanation: Headless Services set `clusterIP: None` so DNS returns Pod IPs (and StatefulSet unique records). ClusterIP would be a single VIP. LoadBalancer is external. ExternalName is a CNAME.

questions.objective: Define and enforce Network Policies
questions.stem: A NetworkPolicy should isolate only backend-tier Pods and allow ingress from frontend-tier Pods in the same namespace. Which two spec fields implement that targeting? Select two.
questions.explanation: `spec.podSelector` chooses the Pods the policy applies to. `spec.ingress.from.podSelector` names allowed peers. An empty podSelector selects every Pod in the namespace (too broad). ipBlock 0.0.0.0/0 is CIDR allow-all, not a label selector.

questions.objective: Implement storage classes and dynamic volume provisioning
questions.stem: A PVC with `storageClassName: fast` stays Pending with “no persistent volumes available” and no provisioner logs. The StorageClass exists. What field on the class names the CSI driver that should create the volume?
questions.explanation: `provisioner` (or CSI `provisioner` string) selects the driver. `reclaimPolicy` is Delete/Retain after release. `volumeBindingMode` is Immediate vs WaitForFirstConsumer. `allowVolumeExpansion` is resize.

questions.objective: Implement storage classes and dynamic volume provisioning
questions.stem: A zonal disk must be created in the zone where the Pod actually schedules. Which StorageClass `volumeBindingMode` waits for a Pod?
questions.explanation: `WaitForFirstConsumer` delays binding/provisioning until a Pod is scheduled. `Immediate` provisions as soon as the PVC is created, often in a random zone. Retain/Delete are reclaim policies, not binding modes.

questions.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
questions.stem: If a StorageClass omits `reclaimPolicy`, Kubernetes defaults it to Delete.
questions.explanation: Documented default reclaimPolicy for StorageClass is Delete. Retain must be set explicitly. True.

questions.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
questions.stem: A PVC is `ReadWriteOnce`. Two Pods on two different nodes both mount it. What happens?
questions.explanation: RWO is one *node*. A second node cannot attach. RWO is not per-Pod (that is ReadWriteOncePod, which is even stricter). Repeating the access mode in the PVC does not change the rule. hostPath is a different volume type.

choices.text: Both nodes mount read-write because RWO means one writer per *Pod*
Both succeed if they use `accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]` twice
The second Pod can mount if it uses `ReadWriteOncePod`
Only one node can attach; the other Pod stays Pending or errors on attach

questions.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
questions.stem: Several Pods on different nodes must write the same filesystem. Which access mode must the PV/PVC support?
questions.explanation: ReadWriteMany (RWX) is multi-node read-write. RWO is single-node. ROX is multi-node read-only. Filesystem vs block is volumeMode, not access mode.

questions.objective: Manage persistent volumes and persistent volume claims
questions.stem: A PVC requests 10Gi, `ReadWriteOnce`, storageClass `fast`. A matching unbound PV exists. What binds them?
questions.explanation: The control plane bind controller matches PVC to PV (capacity, access modes, class, selectors). You do not kubectl-bind. A Deployment does not bind volumes. CSI node plugin mounts after bind.

choices.text: The Deployment controller binds PVs at create
kubelet binds before the PVC exists
The PV controller binds matching PV and PVC

questions.objective: Manage persistent volumes and persistent volume claims
questions.stem: A PVC is Bound. The Pod that used it was deleted. The PVC object is still there. What is the PV status typically?
questions.explanation: Bound stays Bound while the PVC exists. Released happens after the PVC is deleted (then reclaimPolicy applies). Available is unbound. Failed is an error state.

questions.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
questions.stem: A Pod needs scratch space that lasts for the Pod’s life and is deleted when the Pod is deleted. Which volume type?
questions.explanation: emptyDir is Pod-lifetime scratch. A PVC/PV outlives the Pod. hostPath is a node path and survives. configMap is read-mostly config files.

questions.objective: Implement storage classes and dynamic volume provisioning
questions.stem: A PVC's requested size was increased. The filesystem did not grow. The StorageClass allows expansion. What else is commonly required?
questions.explanation: The CSI driver must support expansion (and the fs may need a remount/restart). volumeBindingMode is not a PVC field and does not resize. allowVolumeExpansion lives on the StorageClass, not the PV. RWX is an access mode, not a resize switch.

choices.text: A CSI driver that implements expansion

questions.objective: Manage persistent volumes and persistent volume claims
questions.stem: A PVC must bind only to PVs labeled `media=ssd`. Which PVC field expresses that?
questions.explanation: `spec.selector` on the PVC matches PV labels. storageClassName selects a class. volumeName pins a specific PV name. annotations are not the bind selector.

questions.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
questions.stem: A PV has `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain`. The PVC is deleted. What happens to the data?
questions.explanation: Retain keeps data; the PV becomes Released until an admin reclaims it. Delete would remove the backend. Recycle is deprecated. Kubernetes does not copy volume contents into etcd.

choices.text: The PV becomes Released and the data remains until an admin reclaims it
The provisioner deletes the backend because Delete is always forced
The provisioner deletes the backend disk

questions.objective: Implement storage classes and dynamic volume provisioning
questions.stem: A PVC omits `storageClassName` and still binds dynamically. How was the class chosen?
questions.explanation: The default StorageClass (annotation `storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`) is used when the PVC omits a name. There is no `kubectl default-storageclass` command. The first PV alphabetically is not the rule. kube-public is unrelated.

choices.text: The PV whose name sorts first

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: A Pod is Pending. `kubectl describe pod` shows `FailedScheduling: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory`. What do you change first?
questions.explanation: FailedScheduling Insufficient memory means requests do not fit. Lower requests or add/free memory. ImagePullBackOff is a later phase. A livenessProbe is not used until the Pod runs. Adding a probe does not add node memory.

choices.text: Adjust memory requests or add/free node memory

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: A Pod is stuck. Which kubectl subcommand prints Events, Conditions, and allocated node on that object?
questions.explanation: `kubectl describe` shows events and status. `logs` is stdout. `exec` is a shell. `attach` is a stream. describe is the first stop for Pending/FailedScheduling.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: A Node is NotReady. `kubectl describe node` shows kubelet stopped posting ready. Where do you look on the node next?
questions.explanation: kubelet (journalctl/systemctl) and its logs are the next stop for NotReady. CoreDNS is cluster DNS, not node heartbeat. A missing default StorageClass does not mark nodes NotReady. Ingress is L7.

choices.text: kubelet service/logs on that node (`journalctl -u kubelet`)

questions.objective: Manage and evaluate container output streams
questions.stem: A Pod is CrashLoopBackOff with restart count rising. Which command shows the *current* container instance's stdout?
questions.explanation: `kubectl logs` is the current instance. `-p` is the previous crashed instance (a different item). describe is events. exec often fails while the container is crashing. drain is node maintenance.

choices.text: `kubectl exec -it -- bash` as the only step

questions.objective: Manage and evaluate container output streams
questions.stem: The current container instance just started and is empty. You need stdout from the instance that crashed. Which logs flag?
questions.explanation: `--previous` (`-p`) is the last terminated instance. `-f` follows the current stream. `--all-containers` is every container in the Pod, still current. `--insecure-skip-tls-verify` is TLS.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: A Pod is ImagePullBackOff. describe shows `pull access denied`. Which spec field is the usual fix for a private registry?
questions.explanation: Private registry 403s are usually missing imagePullSecrets on the Pod or ServiceAccount. IfNotPresent still pulls when the image is absent. livenessProbe and hostNetwork do not authenticate to a registry.

choices.text: `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` with a never-pulled private image

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: Which kubectl subcommand evicts Pods from a node before maintenance (respecting PDBs)?
questions.explanation: `kubectl drain` cordons and evicts. `cordon` only marks unschedulable. `delete node` removes the object. `taint` is a different mechanism.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: You need to stop new Pods landing on `node-1` but leave existing Pods running. Which command?
questions.explanation: `kubectl cordon` marks Unschedulable without evicting. `drain` also evicts. `delete node` removes the Node. `uncordon` re-enables scheduling.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: A node was cordoned. Which kubectl subcommand marks it schedulable again?
questions.explanation: `kubectl uncordon <node>` clears the unschedulable taint/flag. drain/cordon do the opposite.

questions.objective: Monitor cluster and application resource usage
questions.stem: `kubectl top nodes` fails with “Metrics API not available”. Which component is missing?
questions.explanation: metrics-server (or another metrics API) backs `kubectl top`. CoreDNS is DNS. kube-proxy is Services. The dashboard is a UI and is not required for the metrics API.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: You want recent cluster Events sorted by time in namespace `prod`. Which command is the usual one?
questions.explanation: `kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` (or `describe` on the object). `logs -n prod` is container stdout, not Events. `top` is metrics. `auth can-i` is RBAC.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: kubectl hangs talking to the cluster. On a kubeadm control-plane node, which static Pod/process do you inspect first for API failures?
questions.explanation: kube-apiserver is the API. kube-scheduler places Pods. kube-proxy is data-plane Services. CoreDNS is DNS. Check the static Pod logs in kube-system / crictl / journal.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot services and networking
questions.stem: CoreDNS is Running but `kubernetes.default.svc` does not resolve from a test Pod. `kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns` shows ClusterIP. What is a common next check?
questions.explanation: If CoreDNS Pods run, check that the kube-dns Service has Ready endpoints and that CoreDNS logs are clean (config, upstream). Service type does not need to be NodePort. StorageClass and metrics-server are unrelated to cluster DNS.

choices.text: The cluster has no default StorageClass
CoreDNS Service type should be NodePort
Endpoints/EndpointSlices for kube-dns and CoreDNS logs/errors

questions.objective: Troubleshoot services and networking
questions.stem: Clients hit Service `web` and hang. `kubectl get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web` is empty. Pods named `web-*` are Running. What is the usual mismatch?
questions.explanation: Empty EndpointSlices mean selector mismatch or not-Ready Pods. targetPort mismatch still lists Ready Pods; traffic would fail after that. ClusterIP type still has endpoints. NetworkPolicy drops packets, it does not empty EndpointSlices.

choices.text: The Service type must not be ClusterIP
`targetPort` does not match the container port, so EndpointSlices stay empty
Service selector does not match Pod labels, or Pods are not Ready

questions.objective: Troubleshoot services and networking
questions.stem: After adding a default-deny NetworkPolicy, Pods cannot resolve Service names. Egress was not allowed to CoreDNS. What should the policy allow?
questions.explanation: Cluster DNS is UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS. 6443 is the API, not DNS. NodePort 30000 is not DNS. Removing kube-proxy does not restore DNS through a default-deny egress policy.

choices.text: Egress to the API server port only

questions.objective: Manage and evaluate container output streams
questions.stem: You need a shell in a running container named `app` in Pod `web-0`. Which command?
questions.explanation: `kubectl exec -it web-0 -c app -- /bin/sh` is the documented pattern. logs is stdout. attach is the primary process, not a new shell. port-forward is networking.

questions.objective: Manage and evaluate container output streams
questions.stem: Which kubectl subcommand prints a container’s stdout/stderr stream?
questions.explanation: `kubectl logs` is the output stream. describe is object details. exec is a process. attach attaches the primary process TTY.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot services and networking
questions.stem: On one worker, ClusterIP Service VIPs do not respond; Pod IPs still ping. kube-proxy Pods show 0 restarts. What is a useful next check on that node?
questions.explanation: If kube-proxy is 'Running' but Services fail on one node, inspect whether iptables or IPVS actually has the Service rules (wrong mode, failed sync). CoreDNS is not per-worker. etcd and metrics-server do not run on workers in kubeadm.

choices.text: etcd member list on the worker
iptables/IPVS rules kube-proxy should have programmed (`iptables-save` / `ipvsadm`)

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: kube-scheduler on a kubeadm control plane is CrashLooping. You already know the static manifest path. What is the usual next log source?
questions.explanation: The static Pod still has kubelet-collected logs via kubectl/crictl. CoreDNS is another component. PKI files are certificates. Helm notes are not kubeadm's scheduler.

choices.text: `kubectl logs` on the kube-scheduler Pod in kube-system (or crictl logs)
Files under `/etc/kubernetes/pki` as the log file

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: On a node, `kubectl` cannot talk to the API. You still need to list containers the runtime is running. Which node tool talks CRI to containerd?
questions.explanation: crictl is the CRI CLI kubelet uses. ctr/nerdctl talk containerd; docker talks dockerd. If the node is CRI-only, docker ps is the wrong daemon. kubectl/helm need the API, which is down in this scenario.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: `kubectl drain node-1` hangs: “cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod’s disruption budget”. What object is blocking the drain?
questions.explanation: PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable/maxUnavailable is the documented drain blocker. NetworkPolicy does not block eviction. LimitRange is admission. a Service does not implement PDB.

questions.objective: Monitor cluster and application resource usage
questions.stem: A container was OOMKilled. `kubectl describe pod` shows `Last State: OOMKilled`. Which spec field is the usual knob to raise?
questions.explanation: OOMKill is the cgroup limit (`resources.limits.memory`). Raising only requests without a limit (or with a still-too-low limit) does not stop the kill. CPU limits do not OOMKill. replicas is count, not memory.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot services and networking
questions.stem: A livenessProbe starts failing after the Pod has been Ready for an hour. What does kubelet do to that container?
questions.explanation: liveness failure restarts the container. Readiness failure only drops endpoints (that is a different probe). kubelet does not cordon the node or delete the Pod object from etcd.

choices.text: Restarts the container (CrashLoop if it keeps failing)
Only removes the Pod from Service endpoints and never restarts it
Deletes the Pod object from etcd

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: You need kube-controller-manager logs on a kubeadm control plane. Which source is the usual one?
questions.explanation: kubeadm runs controller-manager as a static Pod; logs are `kubectl logs` on that Pod (or crictl). journalctl -u kube-controller-manager is the wrong unit—kubelet runs the static Pod. CoreDNS is a different component. PKI files are certs, not logs.

choices.text: `kubectl logs` on the kube-controller-manager Pod in kube-system

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: `kubectl get nodes` returns `Forbidden`. The cluster is healthy for cluster-admin. What do you inspect for this user?
questions.explanation: Forbidden is RBAC (or ABAC/webhook authz). CNI would not produce Forbidden on get nodes. A missing metrics-server is a metrics error. An empty EndpointSlice is Services.

choices.text: Roles/ClusterRoles and Bindings for that user/SA

questions.objective: Manage and evaluate container output streams
questions.stem: Pod `web-0` has containers `app` and `sidecar`. `kubectl logs web-0` errors that a container must be specified. How do you get `app` stdout?
questions.explanation: `-c app` selects the container. `--previous` is the last crash. `--all-namespaces` is the wrong axis. `exec` is a shell, not logs.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
questions.stem: You want a live check that kube-apiserver is serving on a control-plane node without kubectl config. Which local endpoint is the usual healthz?
questions.explanation: kube-apiserver `/healthz` (and `/livez`, `/readyz`) on the secure port (6443) is the documented health. kubelet 10250 is not the API health. etcd 2379 is etcd. NodePort 30000 is Services.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot services and networking
questions.stem: A Pod must resolve in-cluster Service names such as `kubernetes.default.svc`. Which `dnsPolicy` uses CoreDNS (the usual default for Pods)?
questions.explanation: ClusterFirst sends cluster-domain queries to CoreDNS. Default uses the node's resolv.conf, so cluster names miss. None requires explicit dnsConfig. hostNetwork also typically uses node DNS unless you set ClusterFirstWithHostNet.

questions.objective: Manage role based access control (RBAC)
questions.stem: A Role must let a CI ServiceAccount ship Deployments without removing them. Which two verbs belong in `rules[].verbs`? Select two.
questions.explanation: create and update (often with patch/get/list) ship workloads. delete removes them. impersonate is a different authorization on users/SAs, not on the apps/v1 Deployment resource.

questions.objective: Understand the primitives used to create robust, self-healing, application deployments
questions.stem: A stateless HTTP app must reschedule if a node dies and restart if the process hangs. Which two primitives work together? Select two.
questions.explanation: A Deployment keeps replica count when a node dies. A livenessProbe restarts a hung container. A Job is run-to-completion. A CronJob fires on a schedule, it does not supervise a long-running HTTP process.

questions.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
questions.stem: Which two Service types also allocate a ClusterIP in-cluster (in addition to extra exposure)? Select two.
questions.explanation: NodePort and LoadBalancer still have a ClusterIP plus node ports / external LB. ExternalName is a CNAME. Headless has no ClusterIP.

questions.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
questions.stem: Which two access modes allow more than one node to mount the volume? Select two.
questions.explanation: ROX and RWX are multi-node. RWO is single-node. volumeMode Filesystem vs Block is not an access mode.

questions.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
questions.stem: A Node is Ready but you suspect kubelet is overloaded. Which two node-local signals help confirm that before draining? Select two.

choices.text: `kubectl taint` with NoExecute as the first step

questions.explanation: kubelet logs and node Conditions/allocatable vs allocated are the inspect pair. drain is maintenance after you decide to evacuate. A NoExecute taint is a disruption, not a first diagnostic.

questions.objective: Configure workload autoscaling
questions.stem: An HPA must scale Deployment `api`. Which field names that Deployment?

choices.text: `metadata.ownerReferences` on the HPA pointing at a Node

questions.explanation: HPA.scaleTargetRef points at the scale subresource (Deployment, ReplicaSet, etc.). A Service selector is traffic, not replicas. ownerReferences on a Node is wrong. jobTemplate is a CronJob field.

questions.objective: Understand connectivity between Pods
questions.stem: Pod A sends to Pod B's IP. No Service is involved. Does kube-proxy's iptables Service rules need to match for that packet?

choices.text: No; Pod-to-Pod uses the CNI network, not Service ClusterIP rules
Yes; every Pod IP is a ClusterIP
Yes; kube-proxy NATs all overlay traffic to NodePorts

questions.explanation: Pod IPs are routed by CNI. kube-proxy only handles Service VIP/NodePort/LB mappings. Pod IPs are not ClusterIPs. etcd does not forward packets.
